stops.name: Rammenau, the ribbon-weaver's cottage in Lusatian Saxony
stops.campa: On 19 May 1762, in the village of Rammenau on the edge of the Lusatian hills, a first son is born to Christian Fichte, ribbon-weaver, and his wife Dorothea. The boy is set young to the loom, threading the narrow bands his father sells at market. But he is also sent out over the meadows to keep the village geese, and there, alone with the birds and the sky, the goose-boy carries in his head whole sermons of the pastor Wagner, heard once and held entire. The child who will one day summon a nation opens his eyes among weavers.

stops.name: Rammenau, the sermon recited back entire
stops.campa: One Sunday the Freiherr Ernst Haubold von Miltitz, lord of the estate, rides over from a neighbouring village to hear the famous preacher of Rammenau, and comes too late; the sermon is done. The villagers tell him of the weaver's boy who can give back any sermon he has heard. The goose-boy is fetched from the fields, planted before the baron, and recites the whole discourse from memory, in the very cadence of the pastor, forgetting nothing. The patron is astonished. In that hour the wager of Fichte's life is won: the nobleman resolves to educate him.

stops.name: Meißen, the town school, the patron's gift begun
stops.campa: Von Miltitz keeps his word. The weaver's son, torn from loom and geese, is lodged first with the pastor Krebel at Niederau, then set to the town school of Meißen on the Elbe. The boy who owned nothing but a memory now owns Latin declensions and the first rungs of a learning no ribbon-weaver's son had any right to climb. The patron pays; the child works; the ascent has begun that will end in a lecture-hall under French bayonets.

stops.name: Schulpforta, the princely school by Naumburg
stops.campa: At twelve the boy enters Schulpforta, the severe old monastic Fürstenschule below Naumburg, harshest and most famous of Saxon schools: the same cloister-walls that will one day form Nietzsche. Here the peasant's son drills Greek and Latin among the sons of gentlemen, alone, proud, poor. He reads Lessing in secret and dreams of standing free before the whole world. The discipline is iron; the loneliness deep. But the goose-boy is now a scholar, and the loom is far behind.

stops.name: Jena, the theology student, the patron dead
stops.campa: In 1780 Fichte matriculates at Jena to read theology, then removes to Leipzig. But the good baron von Miltitz dies, and with him the money; the heirs let the support lapse. The gifted student is thrown back on nothing. He grinds through his studies in bitter want, unable to take a degree, tutoring where he can, always one step from ruin: a poor man's son with a giant's mind and an empty purse.

stops.name: Leipzig, the years of the itinerant tutor
stops.campa: From 1784 Fichte drifts from house to house across Saxony as a private tutor, teaching other men's children the letters his own genius has outrun. The employment is precarious, the pay thin, the pride wounded. He walks the roads between engagements with almost nothing. Once, in the depth of it, he stands on a bridge and thinks of ending it, then turns instead to hammer his own iron will against fate. Out of this near-despair the philosopher of freedom is forged: the man who will make the self its own author.

stops.name: Zürich, the tutor's post and Johanna Rahn
stops.campa: In autumn 1788, having failed to better himself in Leipzig, Fichte takes a modest post with an innkeeper's family in Zürich. For two years he lives above the lake in the free Swiss city. Here fortune softens: he meets Johanna Rahn, niece of the poet Klopstock, steady and devoted. They pledge themselves. The wandering, half-broken tutor has found the woman who will share every reversal to come, and, at the last, the fever that carries them both away.

stops.name: Leipzig, the lightning of the Critical Philosophy
stops.campa: Back in Leipzig in the summer of 1790, penniless again, Fichte agrees to coach a student through Kant's philosophy: a subject he does not yet know. He opens the Critiques to earn his bread and is struck as by lightning. The doctrine of freedom, of the moral law within, of the self-legislating will, answers the whole hunger of his life. 'I have been living in a new world,' he writes. The tutor is converted; the drifting is over; he has found his master and his cause.
stops.quote: I have been living in a new world ever since reading the Critique of Practical Reason. Propositions which I thought could never be overturned have been overturned for me. Things have been proved to me which I thought could never be proved.

stops.name: Königsberg, the disciple before Kant
stops.campa: Fichte crosses the German lands on foot and by coach to Königsberg to stand before the sage himself. On 4 July 1791 the pilgrim gains his first interview with Kant, and it is cold; the old man is polite, unmoved, and Fichte withdraws stung. He will not be dismissed. In a burning few weeks he writes a whole book applying the Critical method to a question Kant had never treated, the possibility of divine revelation, and lays it before the master as his letter of credit.

stops.name: Königsberg, the anonymous book that makes his name
stops.campa: Kant reads the manuscript and is impressed; he arranges for his own publisher to bring it out. In 1792 the Attempt at a Critique of All Revelation appears, with no name and no preface. Learned Germany, dazzled, takes it for the long-awaited fourth Critique from Kant's own hand. When Kant publicly names the true author, fame breaks over Fichte overnight: the unknown tutor is at a stroke the coming man of German philosophy. The goose-boy has arrived.

stops.name: Zürich, marriage to Johanna Rahn
stops.campa: In October 1793 Fichte returns to Zürich and marries Johanna Rahn, the constant woman of the poor years. Now famous, he spends the Swiss months plunging deeper into the ground of the Critical system, searching for the single first principle from which the whole of knowledge might be spun. The answer forms in him: not a thing, not a fact, but an act: the I that posits itself. He carries this seed toward Jena, where a chair now waits.

stops.name: Jena, the chair and the inaugural lectures
stops.campa: In May 1794 Fichte mounts the podium at Jena, called to the chair vacated by Reinhold, into the very heart of the German philosophical dawn. He opens with public lectures on the vocation of the scholar, and the hall overflows: a hundred, then more, crushed to hear him. He speaks not softly but as a man commanding: philosophy is the deed of a free will, and the calling of the learned is to be the moral teacher of humankind, the raiser of the race.
stops.quote: The scholar is especially destined for society; his class, more than any other, exists only through society and for society; it is therefore his particular duty to cultivate the social talents in an eminent degree.
stops.quote_source: Fichte, Some Lectures Concerning the Scholar's Vocation (1794), Lecture IV
